lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Athens. The year three hundred ninety-nine B.C. An old man is about to drink poison.

lines.speaker: JAIL
lines.text: Socrates. It's time.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Then bring the cup, my friend. And don't look so sad.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Teacher, please! There's still time. We can get you out tonight!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's you. And to understand why he won't run, we need to go back to the day you were born.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Four hundred thirty-five B.C. You're born in the potters' quarter of Athens, the richest city in Greece.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: A boy! Ten days from now, we name him in front of the whole family.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: And one day, he'll vote in the Assembly. Not like me.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: She's right. In this famous democracy, only adult male citizens can vote. Women, slaves and foreigners can't.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: At seven, he starts school. Letters, the lyre, and wrestling.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: A slave walks him there and back. Every single day.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And my sister? Does she go too?

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: She learns at home. Weaving, and running a house. That's Athens.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Then he'd better learn to speak well. Words win votes in this city.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: When you're five, a plague hits the crowded city. Up to a quarter of the people die, even Pericles, Athens' greatest leader.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Stay inside. Don't touch anyone. The gods are angry.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You survive. And at seventeen, you're running pots to the Agora, the beating heart of Athens.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Two jars for the olive seller. And stay away from the barefoot man by the shoemaker's shop.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Why? Is he dangerous?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Worse. He asks questions.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Then why does everyone crowd around him?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Because he's fun to watch. Until he turns the questions on you.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Young man. You carry pots. Tell me, what makes a pot a good pot?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Easy. It doesn't leak.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Good! And what makes a man a good man?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Um. He's rich? Strong? He wins arguments?

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Then a rich man who lies, is good? Hmm. I'm not sure. Are you?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I thought I knew. Now I'm not sure of anything.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Wonderful! That's where wisdom begins. My mother was a midwife. I help people give birth to ideas.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He's short, snub-nosed, wears the same cloak all year, and never writes anything down. Comedy writers love mocking him.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I saw a play about you when I was twelve. The Clouds! You hung in a basket, staring at the sky!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Ha! I stood up in the theater, so people could compare the mask with the real face.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: At least, that's how the legend goes.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Soon, you follow him everywhere. Today, he corners a famous general, Laches.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Laches, you've fought in battles. What is courage?

lines.speaker: LACH
lines.text: Simple. A brave man stands his ground and never runs.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: And soldiers who pull back on purpose, to win the fight later? Are they cowards?

lines.speaker: LACH
lines.text: Well, no. Then courage is, uh, being tough inside?

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Even tough and foolish? Is foolish stubbornness courage?

lines.speaker: LACH
lines.text: By Zeus, Socrates! I know what courage is. I just can't say it!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's the Socratic method. No lectures. Just question after question, until the weak answers fall apart.

lines.speaker: PLATO
lines.text: Teacher, I came here to wrestle. Can I stay and listen instead?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That young wrestler is Plato. He'll write all of this down one day. It's how we know any of it.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Father, are men good because the gods love them? Or do the gods love them because they're good?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Go to your room.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Questioning everything is not always popular at home.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Four sixteen B.C. You're invited to a symposium. A drinking party, with couches, music and wine mixed with water.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Why do we mix the wine with water?

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Only barbarians drink it straight. And this way, the talking lasts till dawn.

lines.speaker: ALC
lines.text: Make room! Where's Socrates?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Is that Alcibiades? The war hero? He's very drunk.

lines.speaker: ALC
lines.text: Friends, this man is like those little statues in the shops. Ugly on the outside. Open him up, and there are gods inside.

lines.speaker: ALC
lines.text: At Potidaea, I was wounded. He stood over me and saved my life. Then he let me take the medal!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Everyone falls asleep before dawn. Socrates simply gets up, and goes to wash, and starts another day of questions.

lines.speaker: CHAER
lines.text: Want to hear why he does all this? I went to the Oracle at Delphi, and asked: is anyone wiser than Socrates?

lines.speaker: CHAER
lines.text: And the priestess said: no one!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: I was puzzled. I know that I know very little. So I went looking for someone wiser.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Politicians, poets, craftsmen. They all thought they knew everything. They didn't.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: So perhaps I'm wiser in one small way. I don't think I know what I don't know.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: There's one problem. Proving powerful people wrong, in public, makes you a lot of enemies.

lines.speaker: XAN
lines.text: Socrates! You talk all day and earn nothing. We have three sons to feed!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: She's right, of course. I never charge for a conversation.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Unlike the paid teachers of his day, the sophists, he never takes money. His family pays the price.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Four hundred four B.C. After twenty-seven years of war, Sparta beats Athens. Thirty tyrants grab power, and kill hundreds.

lines.speaker: HER
lines.text: Socrates! Go to Salamis, arrest a man named Leon, and bring him here to die.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: No. I won't do something unjust.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Teacher, weren't you afraid they'd kill you?

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: No one knows if death is bad. But doing wrong? That, I know, is bad.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He just walks home. The tyrants fall before they can punish him. But some of them had been his students. And Athens remembers.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Three ninety-nine B.C. Democracy is back. And so are the enemies. Five hundred and one jurors. One day. One verdict.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Jurors are picked at random by a stone machine called a kleroterion, so no one can bribe them in advance.

lines.speaker: MEL
lines.text: Socrates does not honor the city's gods. And he corrupts the young!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He means us. His students.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Meletus, tell us. Who makes the young better?

lines.speaker: MEL
lines.text: The laws!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: And who else? The jurors? The Assembly? Everyone in Athens, except me?

lines.speaker: MEL
lines.text: Exactly!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Then the young are very lucky. Only one corrupter, and thousands of helpers.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Men of Athens, I will never stop asking questions. The unexamined life is not worth living.

lines.speaker: HER
lines.text: The jury has voted. Two hundred and eighty, guilty. Two hundred and twenty, not guilty.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Thirty more votes, and I'd be free. As punishment, I propose free dinners for life, like an Olympic champion.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The jury doesn't laugh. Even more of them vote for death.

lines.speaker: CRITO
lines.text: Socrates, listen. The guards are paid. A boat is ready. You can live in Thessaly.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Crito, I've lived seventy years under the laws of Athens. Shall I break them now, to save myself?

lines.speaker: XAN
lines.text: Oh Socrates! This is the last time you'll talk with your friends!

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Crito, have someone take her home. Gently.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: How can you be so calm?

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Death is either a dreamless sleep, or a journey to meet the great souls before us. Either way, why fear it?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He drinks the hemlock calmly. His legs grow heavy, and he lies down.

lines.speaker: SOC
lines.text: Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay it. Don't forget.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Those are his last words.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But the questions don't die. Plato opens a school, the Academy. His student Aristotle teaches Alexander the Great.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Today, law schools and classrooms still use the Socratic method, nearly two thousand four hundred years later.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He never wrote a single word. We wrote them for him.

lines.speaker: PLATO
lines.text: Everything I wrote, I put in his mouth. He's the hero of almost all my dialogues.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you'd been there, would you have followed him? Or voted against him? Tell me in the comments.
